title: The Rise of the Nones
objective: After this level you can explain who the religiously unaffiliated are and why "none" rarely means no belief at all.
summary: US nones rose from 16% in 2007 to 29% in 2023-24, then plateaued. Most choose 'nothing in particular', and most believe in God or a higher power.

cards.headline: Almost a third of American adults now answer "none". Most aren't atheists.
cards.body: Who are the religiously unaffiliated, and what do they actually believe? The answers upend a few assumptions.

cards.headline: A generation of change
cards.body: Pew's Religious Landscape Studies ask tens of thousands of Americans about their faith; the latest surveyed 36,908 adults. The religiously unaffiliated were 16% of adults in 2007, 23% in 2014 and 29% in 2023-24. Then the climb paused: Pew reports the share has plateaued in recent years. Meanwhile 19% of US adults were raised Christian and now call themselves unaffiliated.

cards.headline: Three kinds of none
cards.body: Remember Level 9's survey box? "None" gathers three different answers. In Pew's 2023 data, 17% of nones called themselves atheist and 20% agnostic. The other 63%, by far the biggest group, chose "nothing in particular". So the typical none isn't a committed atheist. They're someone who doesn't claim a religious label.

cards.headline: Believing without belonging
cards.body: Most nones, Pew found, believe in God or some other higher power. About half say spirituality is very important in their lives or think of themselves as spiritual. None, it turns out, rarely means nothing.

cards.headline: Why they dropped the label
cards.body: Asked why they aren't religious, two-thirds of nones say they question a lot of religious teachings or don't believe in God. And 47% say disliking religious organizations is a very important reason. For many, the quarrel is with institutions, not only with ideas.

cards.headline: The Rise of the Nones: the takeaways

options.label: humanist

options.rationale: They are one of the three kinds of none.
